Haggai. Four dated words in the second year of Darius: build the house.

Haggai 1:4 (KJV) →
HOW THE WORD KEPT COMING
The word of the LORD came “by Haggai the prophet”, and once “unto Haggai”. Haggai 1:1 Haggai 1:3 Haggai 2:1 Haggai 2:10 Haggai 2:20
He is called “the LORD’s messenger in the LORD’s message”, and the people obeyed his words “as the LORD their God had sent him”. Haggai 1:12–13

He put two questions of the law to the priests, whether holy flesh makes food holy and whether one unclean by a dead body makes it unclean, and drew the lesson: “So is this people, and so is this nation before me”. Haggai 2:11–14

Ezra says “Haggai the prophet, and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied unto the Jews that were in Judah and Jerusalem”, and that when the building began again “the prophets of God” were “helping them”. Ezra 5:1–2
From the textEvery word in the book is dated to the day. Haggai 1:1 Haggai 2:1 Haggai 2:10 Haggai 2:20

Scholars' viewKeil (1868) takes this Darius to be Darius Hystaspes (Darius I): Zechariah, he writes, began “in the second year of Darius Hystaspes, only two months later than his contemporary Haggai”. On Parker and Dubberstein's tables (1942), the second year of Darius I began on 3 April 520 BC, and the first day of its sixth month, the day of Haggai's first word, fell on 29 August 520 BC. Haggai 1:1 [37][24]

HOW THE STORY ENDS
Scripture says, tradition says
SCRIPTURE SAYS

From the textHaggai's last dated word is the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month of Darius's second year. Ezra adds that the house was finished in Darius's sixth year through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah. Scripture says nothing more of him. Haggai 2:20 Ezra 6:14–15
TRADITION SAYS

According to tradition, as the Jewish Encyclopedia reports it, Haggai “was born in Chaldea during the Captivity, and was among those that returned under Zerubbabel”, and is numbered among “the men of the Great Synagogue” (Talmud, Baba Batra 15a).[32] Who says so: Jewish tradition, as reported in the Jewish Encyclopedia, reported 1904

His name, the Jewish Encyclopedia notes, stands in the Septuagint titles of some psalms, “though not in all manuscripts alike”.[32] Who says so: Titles in Greek (Septuagint) manuscripts of the Psalms, reported 1904
OPEN QUESTIONS
Where readers have differed
A person: the Messiah
The Targum and the Vulgate, as reported by the Pulpit Commentary; Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871)

The Pulpit Commentary reports that this is “the rendering of the ancient Jewish expositors, the Chaldee Targum, and the Vulgate, which gives, Veniet desideratus cunctis gentibus”, though it notes the difficulty that the verb is plural. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown hold that the Messiah is meant, as the one who satisfies the longings of the nations. Haggai 2:7 [42][41]
The precious things of the nations, brought to the house
C. F. Keil (1868); Ellicott's Commentary; S. R. Driver (1891)

Keil reads it as “the valuable possessions of the heathen, or according to Haggai 2:8 their gold and silver”. Ellicott renders “the precious things of all the nations shall come”, calling the Authorised Version's rendering “grammatically impossible with the present text, for the verb ‘come’ is plural”. Driver speaks of the glory coming from “the munificence of the Gentiles”. Haggai 2:7–8 [23][40][3]
IN SCRIPTURE
Every passage
CHAPTERS · 4
Haggai 1 Haggai 2 Ezra 5 Ezra 6
PASSAGES · 3
Haggai 1:1–2:23 Ezra 5:1–2 Ezra 6:14–15
WHAT SCRIPTURE DOES NOT SAY
Scripture gives Haggai no father, tribe or home.
Haggai 2:3 asks who among the people had seen the house “in her first glory”; it does not say whether Haggai had.
Scripture does not say when or where Haggai died.
